claim: Channelrhodopsins (ChRs) are light-gated ion channels from protists used as optogenetic tools for controlling neurons and cardiomyocytes.
source: Light-gated ion channels from protists (channelrhodopsins or ChRs) are optogenetic tools widely used for controlling neurons and cardiomyocytes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about ChRs and their applications.

claim: Multiplex optogenetic applications require spectrally separated molecules, which are difficult to engineer without disrupting channel function.
source: Multiplex optogenetic applications require spectrally separated molecules, which are difficult to engineer without disrupting channel function.
evidence: This is stated as a known challenge in the field, supported by general knowledge of optogenetics.

claim: Three naturally blue-shifted ChRs from ancyromonads were identified through scanning numerous sequence databases.
source: Scanning numerous sequence databases, we identified three naturally blue-shifted ChRs from ancyromonads.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the bioinformatics methods described.

claim: Ancyromonad ChRs form a separate branch on the phylogenetic tree.
source: They form a separate branch on the phylogenetic tree and contain residue motifs characteristic of anion ChRs (ACRs).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Ancyromonad ChRs contain residue motifs characteristic of anion ChRs (ACRs).
source: They form a separate branch on the phylogenetic tree and contain residue motifs characteristic of anion ChRs (ACRs).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only two of the three ancyromonad ChRs conduct chloride.
source: However, only two conduct chloride, whereas the closely related Nutomonas longa homolog generates inward cation currents in mammalian cells under physiological conditions
evidence: This is supported by ion selectivity experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Nutomonas longa homolog (NlCCR) generates inward cation currents in mammalian cells under physiological conditions.
source: whereas the closely related Nutomonas longa homolog generates inward cation currents in mammalian cells under physiological conditions
evidence: This is supported by patch clamp recordings and ion substitution experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: NlCCR generates inward cation currents that significantly exceed those by previously known tools with similar spectral maxima (peak absorption at ~440 nm).
source: significantly exceeding those by previously known tools with similar spectral maxima (peak absorption at ~440 nm)
evidence: This is supported by comparison with PsChR2 shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ancyromonad ChRs can be activated by near-infrared two-photon illumination.
source: Ancyromonad ChRs could be activated by near-infrared two-photon illumination, a technique that enables the deeper-tissue optogenetic activation of specific neurons in three dimensions.
evidence: This is supported by two-photon excitation experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Both ancyromonad ACRs allowed optogenetic silencing of mouse cortical neurons in brain slices.
source: Both ancyromonad ACRs allowed optogenetic silencing of mouse cortical neurons in brain slices.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology experiments in brain slices shown in Figure 7.

claim: AnsACR expression in cholinergic neurons enabled photoinhibition of pharyngeal muscle contraction in live C. elegans worms.
source: Ancyromonas sigmoides ACR (AnsACR) expression in cholinergic neurons enabled photoinhibition of pharyngeal muscle contraction in live worms.
evidence: This is supported by electropharyngeogram recordings shown in Figure 8.

claim: ChRs were first discovered as photoreceptors guiding phototaxis and photophobic response in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii.
source: ChRs, also known as 'Chlamydomonas sensory rhodopsins', were first discovered as the photoreceptors guiding phototaxis and the photophobic response in the chlorophyte C. reinhardtii (Sineshchekov et al., 2002; Govorunova et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The chromophore in ChRs is attached via a retinylidene Schiff base (RSB) linkage to a conserved lysine residue in the seventh transmembrane helix (TM7).
source: The chromophore is attached via a retinylidene Schiff base (RSB) linkage to a conserved lysine residue in the seventh transmembrane helix (TM7).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ChR structure.

claim: The seven-transmembrane (7TM) domain is sufficient for ChR channel activity.
source: The seven-transmembrane (7TM) domain is sufficient for channel activity; the role of the C-terminal domain, which comprises up to half of the polypeptide chain, remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ChR structure-function relationships.

claim: The role of the C-terminal domain in ChRs, which comprises up to half of the polypeptide chain, remains unclear.
source: The seven-transmembrane (7TM) domain is sufficient for channel activity; the role of the C-terminal domain, which comprises up to half of the polypeptide chain, remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Considerable diversity within the ChR family suggests convergent evolution of light-gated channel function.
source: A considerable diversity within the ChR family suggests a convergent evolution of light-gated channel function (Govorunova et al., 2022c).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to previous work.

claim: ChRs form dimers or trimers.
source: ChRs form dimers (Volkov et al., 2017; Li et al., 2019) or trimers (Tucker et al., 2022; Morizumi et al., 2023)
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: ChR ionic conductance is intrinsic to individual protomers, unlike voltage- or ligand-gated channels where several protomers contribute to the channel pore.
source: but their ionic conductance is intrinsic to individual protomers, unlike voltage- or ligand-gated channels, in which several protomers contribute to the channel pore.
evidence: This is stated as a distinguishing feature of ChRs compared to other channels, based on established knowledge.

claim: Anion channelrhodopsins (ACRs) generate photoinduced anion influx in mammalian cells.
source: Anion channelrhodopsins (ACRs) generate photoinduced anion influx in mammalian cells; cation channelrhodopsins (CCRs) generate H+ and Na+ influx; and kalium channelrhodopsins (KCRs) generate K+ efflux (Govorunova et al., 2022a, Govorunova et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cation channelrhodopsins (CCRs) generate H+ and Na+ influx.
source: Anion channelrhodopsins (ACRs) generate photoinduced anion influx in mammalian cells; cation channelrhodopsins (CCRs) generate H+ and Na+ influx; and kalium channelrhodopsins (KCRs) generate K+ efflux (Govorunova et al., 2022a, Govorunova et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Kalium channelrhodopsins (KCRs) generate K+ efflux.
source: Anion channelrhodopsins (ACRs) generate photoinduced anion influx in mammalian cells; cation channelrhodopsins (CCRs) generate H+ and Na+ influx; and kalium channelrhodopsins (KCRs) generate K+ efflux (Govorunova et al., 2022a, Govorunova et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: ACRs and KCRs are used for optogenetic neuronal inhibition.
source: ACRs and KCRs are used for optogenetic neuronal inhibition, and CCRs are used for neuronal activation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about optogenetic applications.

claim: CCRs are used for neuronal activation.
source: ACRs and KCRs are used for optogenetic neuronal inhibition, and CCRs are used for neuronal activation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about optogenetic applications.

claim: Even the most red-shifted ChRs retain sufficient sensitivity to blue light due to their relatively wide spectral bandwidth.
source: Even the most red-shifted ChRs retain sufficient sensitivity to blue light due to their relatively wide spectral bandwidth (Oda et al., 2018; Govorunova et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Development of red-light-absorbing genetically encoded fluorescent biosensors for monitoring neural activity opened up the possibility of pairing them with blue-shifted ChRs.
source: The development of red-light-absorbing genetically encoded fluorescent biosensors for monitoring neural activity (Sakamoto and Yokoyama, 2025) opened up the possibility of pairing them with blue-shifted ChRs.
evidence: This is an inference based on technological developments, supported by citation.

claim: Molecular engineering yielded several blue-shifted ChRs, but mutagenetic perturbations of the binding pocket frequently harm channel function.
source: Molecular engineering yielded several blue-shifted ChRs (Kato et al., 2015), but mutagenetic perturbations of the binding pocket frequently harm channel function.
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents a known limitation of engineering approaches.

claim: Approximately ~1000 ChR sequences are currently known, but a much smaller number has been functionally characterized.
source: Approximately ~1000 ChR sequences are currently known, but a much smaller number has been functionally characterized (Govorunova et al., 2022c).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Ancyromonads represent a distinct major clade near the most commonly inferred root of the eukaryote tree.
source: Ancyromonads (also known as planomonads) represent a distinct major clade near the most commonly inferred root of the eukaryote tree (Brown et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to phylogenetic work.

claim: ChR homologs were identified in Ancyromonas sigmoides, Fabomonas tropica, and Nutomonas longa through bioinformatic search.
source: Our bioinformatic search identified ChR homologs in the ancyromonads Ancyromonas sigmoides, Fabomonas tropica, and Nutomonas longa
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the bioinformatics methods described.

claim: ChR homologs were identified in Ancoracysta twista, a predatory flagellate placed in the newly established supergroup Provora.
source: Ancoracysta twista, a predatory flagellate placed in the newly established supergroup Provora (Tikhonenkov et al., 2022)
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatics search and citation.

claim: ChR homologs were identified in the diatom Odontella aurita.
source: the diatom Odontella aurita
evidence: This is a finding from the bioinformatics search.

claim: ChR homologs were identified in Paraphysoderma sedebokerense, a chytrid-like fungus from the phylum Blastocladiomycota.
source: and Paraphysoderma sedebokerense, a chytrid-like fungus from the phylum Blastocladiomycota.
evidence: This is a finding from the bioinformatics search.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis placed the ancyromonad ChRs on a separate branch of the ACR tree together with their metagenomic homologs from the TARA Oceans database.
source: Phylogenetic analysis placed the ancyromonad ChRs on a separate branch of the ACR tree together with their metagenomic homologs from the TARA Oceans database (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The A. twista and O. aurita homologs clustered with known stramenopile ACRs.
source: The A. twista and O. aurita homologs clustered with known stramenopile ACRs.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The P. sedebokerense sequence showed only a distant homology to previously known ACRs.
source: The P. sedebokerense sequence showed only a distant homology to previously known ACRs.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: All ancyromonad ChR sequences exhibit a non-carboxylate residue at the primary counterion position, corresponding to Asp85 in TM3 of Halobacterium salinarum bacteriorhodopsin.
source: All these sequences exhibit a non-carboxylate residue at the primary counterion position, corresponding to Asp85 in TM3 of Halobacterium salinarum bacteriorhodopsin (BR), marked by the red arrow in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, as found in all known ACRs.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The second carboxylate in the photoactive site, corresponding to Asp212 of BR, is replaced with Glu in the N. longa sequence.
source: The second carboxylate in the photoactive site, contributed by TM7 and corresponding to Asp212 of BR, is replaced with Glu in the N. longa sequence
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The second carboxylate in the photoactive site is replaced with Gln in the P. sedebokerense sequence.
source: and with Gln in the P. sedebokerense sequence (the blue arrow in Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: All three ancyromonad ChRs generated robust photocurrents when expressed in HEK293 cells.
source: All three ancyromonad ChRs generated robust photocurrents and showed maximal sensitivity in the blue spectral range (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by patch clamp recordings shown in Figure 1B.

claim: All three ancyromonad ChRs showed maximal sensitivity in the blue spectral range.
source: All three ancyromonad ChRs generated robust photocurrents and showed maximal sensitivity in the blue spectral range (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by action spectra shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The A. sigmoides homolog was named AnsACR based on its anion selectivity.
source: Based on their ionic selectivities (see the next section), we named the A. sigmoides, F. tropica, and N. longa homologs AnsACR, FtACR, and NlCCR, respectively.
evidence: This is based on ion selectivity experiments described in the next section.

claim: The F. tropica homolog was named FtACR based on its anion selectivity.
source: Based on their ionic selectivities (see the next section), we named the A. sigmoides, F. tropica, and N. longa homologs AnsACR, FtACR, and NlCCR, respectively.
evidence: This is based on ion selectivity experiments described in the next section.

claim: The N. longa homolog was named NlCCR based on its cation selectivity.
source: Based on their ionic selectivities (see the next section), we named the A. sigmoides, F. tropica, and N. longa homologs AnsACR, FtACR, and NlCCR, respectively.
evidence: This is based on ion selectivity experiments described in the next section.

claim: The A. twista and O. aurita homologs showed spectral sensitivity in the blue-green range.
source: The spectral sensitivity of the A. twista and O. aurita homologs was in the blue-green range (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, left).
evidence: This is supported by action spectra shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Partial replacement of Cl- in the bath with non-permeable aspartate shifted reversal potential to more positive values in A. twista and O. aurita homologs, confirming their anion selectivity.
source: Partial replacement of Cl- in the bath with non-permeable aspartate shifted reversal potential (Vr) to more positive values, confirming their anion selectivity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, middle and right).
evidence: This is supported by ion substitution experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The A. twista homolog was named AtACR.
source: We named them AtACR, OaACR1, and OaACR2.
evidence: This is based on the anion selectivity demonstrated in experiments.

claim: The O. aurita homologs were named OaACR1 and OaACR2.
source: We named them AtACR, OaACR1, and OaACR2.
evidence: This is based on the anion selectivity demonstrated in experiments.

claim: No photocurrents were detected in cells transfected with the P. sedebokerense homolog, although its expression and membrane targeting were evident from tag fluorescence.
source: No photocurrents were detected in cells transfected with the P. sedebokerense homolog, although its expression and membrane targeting were evident from the tag fluorescence.
evidence: This is a negative result from patch clamp experiments.

claim: The P. sedebokerense protein was named ParsR, where R means 'rhodopsin'.
source: Therefore, we named this protein ParsR, where R means 'rhodopsin'.
evidence: This naming is based on the lack of channel activity despite rhodopsin-like properties.

claim: Purified AnsACR, FtACR, and NlCCR proteins yielded 0.25, 0.35, and 0.15 mg per L culture, respectively.
source: yielding 0.25, 0.35, and 0.15 mg purified protein per L culture for AnsACR, FtACR, and NlCCR, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from protein purification experiments.

claim: The absorption spectra of purified ancyromonad ChR proteins were slightly blue-shifted from their respective photocurrent action spectra.
source: The absorption spectra of the purified proteins (Figure 1C) were slightly blue-shifted from the respective photocurrent action spectra (Figure 1—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is supported by comparison of absorption and action spectra shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The discrepancy between absorption and action spectra is likely due to the presence of non-electrogenic cis-retinal-bound forms.
source: likely due to the presence of non-electrogenic cis-retinal-bound forms.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations, supported by citation to similar findings in KCRs.

claim: Co-expression of AnsACR with Chrimson in HEK293 cells resulted in hyperpolarizing photocurrents upon illumination with λ<500 nm and depolarizing photocurrents at longer wavelengths.
source: Figure 1D, black shows that the direction of photocurrents was hyperpolarizing upon illumination with λ<500 nm and depolarizing at longer wavelengths.
evidence: This is supported by action spectra of co-expressed proteins shown in Figure 1D.

claim: A shoulder near 520 nm in the co-expression action spectrum revealed a FRET contribution from EYFP.
source: A shoulder near 520 nm revealed a FRET contribution from EYFP (Govorunova et al., 2020), which was also observed upon expression of the Chrimson construct alone (Figure 1D, red).
evidence: This is an inference based on spectral features, supported by citation and comparison with Chrimson alone.

claim: The current amplitude saturated earlier than the time-to-peak for all tested ancyromonad ChRs.
source: The current amplitude saturated earlier than the time-to-peak for all tested ChRs.
evidence: This is supported by light dependence experiments shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Desensitization at the end of 1-s illumination revealed a complex light dependence in ancyromonad ChRs.
source: Quantitation of desensitization at the end of 1-s illumination revealed a complex light dependence (Figure 1—figure supplement 4F).
evidence: This is supported by desensitization analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4F.

claim: The mean AnsACR photocurrent measured by SyncroPatch was significantly larger than the mean FtACR photocurrent.
source: Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B shows that the mean AnsACR photocurrent measured by the SyncroPatch was significantly larger than the mean FtACR photocurrent
evidence: This is supported by automated patch clamp data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The mean NlCCR photocurrent was significantly larger than that of PsChR2.
source: and the mean NlCCR photocurrent was significantly larger than that of Platymonas subcordiformis channelrhodopsin 2 (PsChR2), a previously known excitatory optogenetic tool with a similar blue-shifted spectrum (Govorunova et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by automated patch clamp data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: AnsACR and FtACR showed similarly negative reversal potential values, suggesting higher relative permeability to Cl- than F-.
source: AnsACR and FtACR showed similarly negative Vr values, suggesting higher relative permeability to Cl- than F-, as earlier found in GtACRs by manual patch clamping (Govorunova et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference from IV curve data shown in Figure 2D-F, supported by citation to similar findings.

claim: The reversal potential values of the peak current and that at the end of illumination were not significantly different for AnsACR and FtACR, indicating no change in relative permeability during illumination.
source: The Vr values of the peak current and that at the end of illumination were not significantly different by the two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test (Figure 2G), indicating no change in the relative permeability during illumination.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of IV curve data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: NlCCR photocurrents reversed near 0 mV.
source: Unexpectedly, the NlCCR photocurrents reversed near 0 mV (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This is supported by IV curve data shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: When Cl- in the external solution was partially replaced with aspartate, only AnsACR and FtACR showed substantial reversal potential shifts to more positive values, confirming their permeability to Cl-.
source: However, when Cl- in the external solution was partially replaced with bulky, non-permeable aspartate, only AnsACR and FtACR showed substantial Vr shifts to more positive values, which confirmed their permeability to Cl-, but no such shift was detected in NlCCR (Figure 2H–J, red symbols).
evidence: This is supported by ion substitution experiments shown in Figure 2H-J.

claim: Upon replacing Cl- with NO3-, AnsACR and FtACR, but not NlCCR, showed reversal potential shifts to more negative values, indicating higher relative permeability to NO3- than to Cl-.
source: Upon replacing Cl- with NO3-, AnsACR and FtACR, but not NlCCR, showed Vr shifts to more negative values (Figure 2H–J, green), as did GtACRs examined by manual patch clamping (Govorunova et al., 2015), which indicated higher relative permeability to NO3- than to Cl-.
evidence: This is supported by ion substitution experiments shown in Figure 2H-J and comparison with GtACRs.

claim: FtACR exhibited a larger reversal potential shift in NO3- than AnsACR.
source: FtACR exhibited a larger Vr shift in NO3- than AnsACR (P=2.6E10-5 by the two-tailed Mann-Whitney test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of ion substitution data.

claim: Replacing Na+ with NMDG+ resulted in a negative reversal potential shift in NlCCR but not in AnsACR or FtACR, suggesting that NlCCR is permeable to Na+.
source: Replacing Na+ with N-methyl-D-gluconate (NMDG+) resulted in a negative Vr shift in NlCCR but not the other tested variants (Figure 2H–J, blue), suggesting that NlCCR is permeable to Na+.
evidence: This is supported by ion substitution experiments shown in Figure 2H-J.

claim: Acidifying the external solution to pH 5.4 did not affect the reversal potential of any ancyromonad ChR.
source: Acidifying the external solution to pH 5.4 or replacing Na+ with K+ did not affect the Vr of any ancyromonad ChR (Figure 2, gray and violet).
evidence: This is supported by ion substitution experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Replacing Na+ with K+ did not affect the reversal potential of any ancyromonad ChR.
source: Acidifying the external solution to pH 5.4 or replacing Na+ with K+ did not affect the Vr of any ancyromonad ChR (Figure 2, gray and violet).
evidence: This is supported by ion substitution experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Only AnsACR and FtACR are anion-selective, but NlCCR conducts monovalent metal cations despite its sequence homology to the other two variants.
source: We conclude that only AnsACR and FtACR are anion-selective, but NlCCR conducts monovalent metal cations despite its sequence homology to the other two variants.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ion selectivity experiments described.

claim: AnsACR and FtACR photocurrents exhibited biphasic rise and decay under single-turnover conditions.
source: AnsACR and FtACR photocurrents exhibited biphasic rise and decay (Figure 3A and D), as the earlier characterized GtACR1 (Sineshchekov et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by laser flash photolysis experiments shown in Figure 3A and D.

claim: The IV curves of all kinetic components of AnsACR and FtACR revealed the same reversal potential values, meaning no ion selectivity changes occur during the single-turnover photocycle.
source: The IV curves of all kinetic components revealed the same Vr values (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B), meaning no ion selectivity changes occur during the single-turnover photocycle.
evidence: This is supported by voltage-dependent analysis of flash-induced photocurrents shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: In contrast to GtACR1, no clear indication of the accumulation of a blue-shifted L intermediate was found in ancyromonad ACRs.
source: In contrast to GtACR1, we could not find a clear indication of the accumulation of a blue-shifted L intermediate.
evidence: This is based on transient absorption measurements shown in Figure 3B and E.

claim: After initial decay of a K-like intermediate, red-shifted absorbance temporally increased in both ancyromonad ACRs, reaching a maximum at 100–200 μs.
source: After an initial (unresolved) decay of a K-like intermediate, red-shifted absorbance temporally increased in both ancyromonad ACRs, reaching a maximum at 100–200 μs (Figure 3B and E, red), that is in the time domain of fast channel opening.
evidence: This is supported by transient absorption measurements shown in Figure 3B and E.

claim: The red-shifted intermediate in ancyromonad ACRs could be a long-lived K or an unusual red-shifted L.
source: This red-shifted intermediate could be a long-lived K or an unusual red-shifted L.
evidence: This is speculation based on the transient absorption data.

claim: In FtACR, an additional slower increase in red-shifted absorbance likely reflected the formation of an O-like intermediate.
source: In FtACR, an additional slower increase in the red-shifted absorbance likely reflected the formation of an O-like intermediate (Figure 3E, red).
evidence: This is an inference based on transient absorption data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Accumulation of the M intermediate in AnsACR was only 10 times slower than channel opening.
source: Accumulation of the M intermediate absorbing in the UV range was only 10 (AnsACR) or 2 times (FtACR) slower than channel opening (Figure 3C and F)
evidence: This is supported by comparison of photocurrent and transient absorption kinetics shown in Figure 3C and F.

claim: Accumulation of the M intermediate in FtACR was only 2 times slower than channel opening.
source: Accumulation of the M intermediate absorbing in the UV range was only 10 (AnsACR) or 2 times (FtACR) slower than channel opening (Figure 3C and F)
evidence: This is supported by comparison of photocurrent and transient absorption kinetics shown in Figure 3C and F.

claim: In GtACR1, M intermediate accumulation was 50 times slower than channel opening.
source: although in GtACR1, it was 50 times slower (Sineshchekov et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison with previously published data, supported by citation.

claim: In contrast to GtACR1, no temporal correlation was found between M formation and fast channel closing or between M decay and slow channel closing in ancyromonad ACRs.
source: Also, in contrast to prior observations in GtACR1, no temporal correlation was found between M formation and fast channel closing and between M decay and slow channel closing in ancyromonad ACRs.
evidence: This is based on comparison of photocurrent and transient absorption kinetics shown in Figure 3.

claim: NlCCR's laser-flash-induced photocurrent kinetics showed single exponential opening and closing in Cl-.
source: In contrast to AnsACR and FtACR, NlCCR's laser-flash-induced photocurrent kinetics showed single exponential opening and closing in Cl- and did not change upon its substitution with Asp- in the bath solution (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by laser flash photolysis experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: NlCCR photocurrent kinetics did not change upon substitution of Cl- with Asp- in the bath solution.
source: In contrast to AnsACR and FtACR, NlCCR's laser-flash-induced photocurrent kinetics showed single exponential opening and closing in Cl- and did not change upon its substitution with Asp- in the bath solution (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by laser flash photolysis experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: pH titration of ancyromonad ChRs revealed two transitions.
source: The titration curves revealed two transitions in all ancyromonad ChRs.
evidence: This is supported by pH titration experiments shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Acidification caused a transition to longer peak absorption wavelengths in ancyromonad ChRs, with pKa1s~3.9, 2, and 3.4 for AnsACR, FtACR, and NlCCR, respectively.
source: Acidification caused a transition to longer peak absorption wavelengths, as expected upon protonation of the counterion, with pKa1s~3.9, 2, and 3.4 for AnsACR, FtACR, and NlCCR, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by pH titration experiments shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: The maximum amplitude of the acidification-induced transition in AnsACR (~8 nm) exactly corresponded to the 8 nm red shift of the photocurrent action spectrum in the AnsACR_D226N mutant.
source: The maximum amplitude of this transition in AnsACR (~8 nm) exactly corresponded to the 8 nm red shift of the photocurrent action spectrum in the AnsACR_D226N mutant (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of pH titration and mutant action spectrum data shown in Figure 4A and D.

claim: The D226N mutation in AnsACR did not suppress photocurrent but simplified its kinetics.
source: The D226N mutation did not suppress photocurrent but simplified its kinetics (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by laser flash photolysis experiments shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Instead of biphasic opening and closing observed in wild-type AnsACR, only two exponentials were sufficient to fit the D226N mutant's current, one for opening and one for closing.
source: Instead of the biphasic opening and closing observed in the WT, only two exponentials were sufficient to fit the D226N mutant's current, one for opening and one for closing.
evidence: This is supported by kinetic analysis of flash-induced photocurrents shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Asp226 plays a role in channel gating in AnsACR.
source: This observation suggested the role of Asp226 in channel gating, which was confirmed by analysis of the voltage dependence of the closing τ (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is an inference supported by voltage-dependent kinetic analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Upon shifting to positive voltages, both components of channel closing accelerated in wild-type AnsACR, but the single-exponential closing slowed in the D226N mutant.
source: Upon shifting to positive voltages, both components of channel closing accelerated in the WT, but the single-exponential closing slowed in the mutant
evidence: This is supported by voltage-dependent kinetic analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Oppositely directed charge movements control channel closing in wild-type AnsACR and the D226N mutant.
source: which suggests that oppositely directed charge movements control channel closing in the WT and the mutant.
evidence: This is an inference based on the voltage-dependent kinetic data.

claim: Further acidification of ancyromonad ChRs caused a transition to shorter wavelengths with similar pKa2s.
source: Further acidification caused a transition to shorter wavelengths with similar pKa2s in both purified ancyromonad ACRs and only a slightly lower pKa2 in NlCCR (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by pH titration experiments shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: The second acidification-induced transition most probably reflects Cl- binding in the photoactive site.
source: It most probably reflects binding Cl- in the photoactive site, as in archaeal rhodopsins (Shimono et al., 2000b).
evidence: This is an inference based on pH titration data and comparison with archaeal rhodopsins, supported by citation.

claim: No blue spectral shift was detected in detergent-purified AnsACR at neutral pH upon an increase in Cl- concentration.
source: On the other hand, in contrast to Natronomonas pharaonis halorhodopsin (Váró et al., 1996), no blue spectral shift was detected in detergent-purified AnsACR at neutral pH upon an increase in the Cl- concentration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by Cl- titration experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The G86E mutation in AnsACR led to the appearance of an additional spectral transition with pKa 7.4 upon pH titration.
source: Mutagenetic introduction of Glu in AnsACR in the position of the primary acceptor in BR (the G86E mutation) led to the appearance of an additional spectral transition with pKa 7.4 upon pH titration of purified protein (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by pH titration of the mutant shown in Figure 4G.

claim: An extremely fast M-like UV-absorbing intermediate absent in wild-type AnsACR was observed in the G86E mutant.
source: An extremely fast M-like UV-absorbing intermediate absent in the WT was observed in the mutant (Figure 4H, red).
evidence: This is supported by transient absorption measurements shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The rise and decay τ of the fast M-like intermediate in AnsACR_G86E corresponded to the rise and decay τ of the fast positive current recorded at 0 mV and neutral pH.
source: Its rise and decay τ corresponded to the rise and decay τ of the fast positive current recorded from AnsACR_G86E at 0 mV and neutral pH, superimposed on the fast negative current reflecting the chromophore isomerization (Figure 4I, upper black trace).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of transient absorption and photocurrent kinetics shown in Figure 4H and I.

claim: The fast positive current in AnsACR_G86E is interpreted as an intramolecular proton transfer to the mutagenetically introduced primary acceptor (Glu86).
source: We interpret this positive current as an intramolecular proton transfer to the mutagenetically introduced primary acceptor (Glu86), which was suppressed by negative voltage (Figure 4I, lower black trace).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the photocurrent data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Acidification increased the amplitude of the fast negative current in AnsACR_G86E ~10-fold.
source: Acidification increased the amplitude of the fast negative current ~10-fold (Figure 4I, black arrow)
evidence: This is supported by pH-dependent photocurrent measurements shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Acidification shifted the reversal potential of the fast negative current in AnsACR_G86E ~100 mV to more depolarized values.
source: and shifted its Vr ~100 mV to more depolarized values (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by voltage-dependent analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The increase in fast negative current upon acidification in AnsACR_G86E can be explained by passive inward movement of the RSB proton along the large electrochemical gradient.
source: This can be explained by passive inward movement of the RSB proton along the large electrochemical gradient.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the pH-dependent photocurrent data.

claim: The G86E mutation suppressed channel current in AnsACR at neutral pH, but acidification of the bath to pH 5.4 recovered it.
source: Remarkably, the G86E mutation suppressed channel current at neutral pH, but acidification of the bath to pH 5.4 recovered it (Figure 4I, red arrow).
evidence: This is supported by pH-dependent photocurrent measurements shown in Figure 4I.

claim: The G86E mutation slowed channel closing in AnsACR sixfold.
source: The full current trace recorded under acidic conditions could be deconvoluted into four components with τ 30 μs, 80 μs, 1.5ms, and 640ms, revealing that the mutation slowed channel closing sixfold.
evidence: This is supported by kinetic analysis of photocurrents under acidic conditions.

claim: Replacement of Cl- with Asp- caused an ~40 mV shift of the channel current's reversal potential in AnsACR_G86E, indicating that the mutant channel remained Cl- selective.
source: Replacement of Cl- with Asp- caused an ~40 mV shift of the channel current's Vr (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), indicating that the mutant channel remained Cl- selective.
evidence: This is supported by ion substitution experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The absence of a negative charge at the site corresponding to BR's primary acceptor is the ultimate condition for anion channel function.
source: These results confirm that the absence of a negative charge at the site corresponding to BR's primary acceptor is the ultimate condition for anion channel function.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the G86E mutant data.

claim: Strong alkalization caused simultaneous depletion of absorption in the visible range, appearance of M-like states, and substantial absorption increase at 297 nm in AnsACR.
source: Strong alkalization caused simultaneous depletion of absorption in the visible range, the appearance of the M-like states (at 368 nm in the wild-type AnsACR and 355 nm in the AnsACR_G86E mutant), and a substantial absorption increase at 297 nm, reflecting deprotonation of the RSB and a strong perturbation of the protein band (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by pH titration of absorption spectra shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The pKa values for RSB deprotonation were 11.1 and 10.7 for wild-type AnsACR and G86E mutant, respectively.
source: Analysis of the pH dependence of three parameters (absorption depletion in the visible range, absorption rise in the M-like states' range, and absorption rise at 297 nm) yielded similar pKa values, which were 11.1 and 10.7 for the WT and G86E, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by pH titration analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The high pKa values for RSB deprotonation may explain the high photostability of AnsACR.
source: These high pKa values may explain the high photostability of this protein, as hundreds of laser flashes did not cause its measurable bleaching.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pKa values and observed photostability.

claim: The glutamate in the middle of TM2 corresponding to Glu68 of GtACR1 is conserved in most ACRs, including FtACR, but is replaced with Gln in AnsACR.
source: The glutamate in the middle of TM2 corresponding to Glu68 of GtACR1 is conserved in most ACRs, including FtACR, but is replaced with Gln in AnsACR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, black arrow).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Q48E mutation in AnsACR accelerated channel closing and slowed channel opening, making the photocurrent rise and decay monophasic.
source: Introducing the Q48E mutation in AnsACR accelerated channel closing and slowed channel opening, making the photocurrent rise and decay monophasic (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by laser flash photolysis experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: NlCCR features three residues typical of red-shifted microbial rhodopsins despite being the most blue-shifted among ancyromonad ChRs.
source: Surprisingly, NlCCR, the most blue-shifted among ancyromonad ChRs, features three residues typical of red-shifted microbial rhodopsins (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence comparison shown in Figure 5A.

claim: NlCCR has Phe at the primary counterion position (Asp85 in BR), also found in RubyACRs from Labyrinthulea, the most red-shifted ChRs identified.
source: The first is Phe at the primary counterion position (Asp85 in BR), also found in RubyACRs from Labyrinthulea, the most red-shifted ChRs so far identified (Govorunova et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by sequence comparison and citation to previous work.

claim: Residues homologous to BR's Met118 and Ala215 are responsible for red-shifted absorption in many microbial rhodopsins.
source: The residues homologous to BR's Met118 near the β-ionone ring and Ala215 preceding the RSB lysine in the polypeptide chain are responsible for red-shifted absorption in many microbial rhodopsins (Shimono et al., 2000a; Engqvist et al., 2015; Oda et al., 2018; Oppermann et al., 2024)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The residues homologous to Met118 and Ala215 are conserved in all three blue-absorbing ancyromonad ChRs.
source: but are conserved in all three blue-absorbing ancyromonad ChRs.
evidence: This is supported by sequence comparison shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The S97F, C133M, and C237A mutations red-shifted the GtACR1 spectrum.
source: As expected, the S97F, C133M, and C237A mutations red-shifted the GtACR1 spectrum (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by action spectra of mutants shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The F104S, M143C, and A242C mutations at corresponding sites in HfACR1 caused large blue spectral shifts.
source: The opposite F104S, M143C, and A242C mutations at the corresponding sites in the RubyACR from Hondaea fermentalgiana (HfACR1) caused large blue spectral shifts (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by action spectra of mutants shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Mutation of the Met118 homolog to Val blue-shifted the HfACR1 spectrum but red-shifted the ancyromonad ChR spectra.
source: The same paradoxical behavior was observed upon mutation of the Met118 homolog to Val, which blue-shifted the HfACR1 spectrum but red-shifted the ancyromonad ChR spectra (Figure 5F–H).
evidence: This is supported by action spectra of mutants shown in Figure 5F-H.

claim: Replacement of the Ala215 homolog with Cys or Ser did not change the AnsACR and FtACR spectra.
source: Replacement of the Ala215 homolog with Cys or Ser did not change the AnsACR and FtACR spectra (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by action spectra of mutants shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The AnsACR_M134A/G and NlCCR_M141A/G mutations did not change the spectra.
source: but the AnsACR_M134A/G and NlCCR_M141A/G mutations did not change the spectra, nor did the FtACR_M140G_V144A mutation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by action spectra of mutants shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: The FtACR_M140G_V144A mutation did not change the spectrum.
source: but the AnsACR_M134A/G and NlCCR_M141A/G mutations did not change the spectra, nor did the FtACR_M140G_V144A mutation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by action spectra of mutants shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: The residue geometry and/or interactions in the retinal-binding pocket in ancyromonad ChRs differ from earlier studied microbial rhodopsins.
source: These observations suggest that the residue geometry and/or interactions in the retinal-binding pocket in ancyromonad ChRs differ from the earlier studied microbial rhodopsins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the unexpected mutational effects observed.

claim: The residue position corresponding to BR's Leu93 is the color switch between blue- and green-absorbing proteorhodopsins.
source: The residue position corresponding to BR's Leu93 is the color switch between blue- and green-absorbing proteorhodopsins (BPRs and GPRs; Man et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: AnsACR exhibits a Gln residue at the position corresponding to BR's Leu93, as do BPRs.
source: AnsACR exhibits a Gln residue in this position, as do BPRs
evidence: This is supported by sequence comparison shown in Figure 5A.

claim: FtACR has Leu at the position corresponding to BR's Leu93, as do GPRs.
source: but FtACR has Leu, as do GPRs
evidence: This is supported by sequence comparison shown in Figure 5A.

claim: NlCCR has Met at the position corresponding to BR's Leu93.
source: and NlCCR has Met (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence comparison shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The FtACR_L96Q mutation blue-shifted the spectrum 20 nm.
source: The FtACR_L96Q and NlCCR_M93Q mutations blue-shifted the spectra 20 and 7 nm, respectively (Figure 5I and J)
evidence: This is supported by action spectra of mutants shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The NlCCR_M93Q mutation blue-shifted the spectrum 7 nm.
source: The FtACR_L96Q and NlCCR_M93Q mutations blue-shifted the spectra 20 and 7 nm, respectively (Figure 5I and J)
evidence: This is supported by action spectra of mutants shown in Figure 5J.

claim: The residue position corresponding to BR's Leu93 contributes to color tuning in ancyromonad ACRs.
source: indicating that this residue position contributes to color tuning in ancyromonad ACRs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutational effects observed.

claim: The S89T, E233D, and P235I mutations red-shifted the NlCCR spectrum.
source: The S89T, E233D, and P235I mutations red-shifted the NlCCR spectrum (Figure 5K)
evidence: This is supported by action spectra of mutants shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Three positions (corresponding to Ser89, Glu233, and Pro235 in NlCCR) contribute to the blue shift of wild-type NlCCR compared with AnsACR and FtACR.
source: indicating that these three positions contribute to the blue shift of wild-type NlCCR compared with AnsACR and FtACR.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutational effects observed.

claim: The T90S mutation did not change the AnsACR spectrum.
source: However, the T90S mutation did not change the AnsACR spectrum
evidence: This is supported by action spectra of mutants shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The D226E mutation caused red spectral shifts in AnsACR.
source: and the D226E mutation and a combination of the two mutations caused red spectral shifts in AnsACR (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by action spectra of mutants shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: All three ancyromonad ChRs generated detectable photocurrents under two-photon excitation.
source: All three ChRs generated detectable photocurrents with action spectra showing maximal responses at ~925 nm for AnsACR, 945 nm for FtACR, and 890 nm for NlCCR (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon excitation experiments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The two-photon action spectrum of AnsACR showed maximal response at ~925 nm.
source: All three ChRs generated detectable photocurrents with action spectra showing maximal responses at ~925 nm for AnsACR, 945 nm for FtACR, and 890 nm for NlCCR (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon excitation experiments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The two-photon action spectrum of FtACR showed maximal response at 945 nm.
source: All three ChRs generated detectable photocurrents with action spectra showing maximal responses at ~925 nm for AnsACR, 945 nm for FtACR, and 890 nm for NlCCR (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon excitation experiments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The two-photon action spectrum of NlCCR showed maximal response at 890 nm.
source: All three ChRs generated detectable photocurrents with action spectra showing maximal responses at ~925 nm for AnsACR, 945 nm for FtACR, and 890 nm for NlCCR (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon excitation experiments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The two-photon excitation wavelengths of ancyromonad ChRs fall within the excitation range of common Ti:Sapphire lasers.
source: These wavelengths fall within the excitation range of common Ti:Sapphire lasers, which are widely used in neuroscience laboratories and can be tuned between ~700 nm and 1020–1300 nm.
evidence: This is stated as a practical consideration based on the measured two-photon action spectra.

claim: All five tested ChR variants (AnsACR, FtACR, NlCCR, GtACR1, and GtACR2) exhibited comparable levels of desensitization at the end of 5 s two-photon illumination.
source: All five tested variants exhibited comparable levels of desensitization at the end of illumination (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon desensitization experiments shown in Figure 6I.

claim: AnsACR- and FtACR-expressing neurons showed resting membrane potential, input resistance, and capacitance similar to typical values of untransfected cortical neurons.
source: AnsACR- and FtACR-expressing neurons showed the resting membrane potential, input resistance, and capacitance (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) similar to the typical values of untransfected cortical neurons (Xue et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology measurements shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and comparison with cited values.

claim: Photoactivation of AnsACR and FtACR suppressed current-evoked action potentials in cortical neurons.
source: When positive currents were injected into the somata to excite neurons, photoactivation of AnsACR and FtACR suppressed the current-evoked action potentials, demonstrating the potency of these proteins as optogenetic silencers of mouse cortical neurons (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by whole-cell current clamp recordings shown in Figure 7.

claim: At rest or when a small negative current was injected, AnsACR- and FtACR-expressing neurons could generate a single action potential at the beginning of photostimulation, possibly caused by axonal depolarization.
source: We also observed that at rest or when a small negative current (e.g. –0.1 nA) was injected, the neurons could generate a single action potential at the beginning of photostimulation (Figure 7A and B), possibly caused by axonal depolarization, as reported in GtACR-expressing neurons (Mahn et al., 2018; Messier et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology recordings shown in Figure 7A and B and comparison with cited observations.

claim: Photoactivation of AnsACR or FtACR induced excitatory post-synaptic currents in ACR- neurons.
source: Indeed, when we recorded from ACR- neurons in the electroporated cortical region, we found that photoactivation of either AnsACR- or FtACR-induced excitatory post-synaptic currents (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, D), similar to other tested light-gated Cl- channels.
evidence: This is supported by voltage clamp recordings shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: The pharyngeal pumping frequency in transgenic worms expressing AnsACR in the dark was not significantly different from wild-type worms.
source: In the presence of 10 mM serotonin required to maintain regular pharyngeal pumping, its frequency in the dark was not significantly different in the transgene and wild-type worms (4.07 ± 0.05 and 4.19 ± 0.08 Hz, respectively, mean ± SEM, n=26 transgenic and 11 wild-type worms, respectively; the p-value by the two-tailed Mann-Whitney test is 0.21)
evidence: This is supported by EPG recordings and statistical analysis.

claim: AnsACR expression did not affect pharyngeal function in C. elegans in the darkness.
source: indicating that AnsACR expression did not affect the pharyngeal function in the darkness.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of significant difference in pumping frequency.

claim: The onset of 470 nm illumination caused immediate inhibition of pharyngeal pumping in transgenic worms fed on bacteria supplemented with all-trans-retinal.
source: The onset of 470 nm illumination caused an immediate inhibition of pumping in such transgene worms but not in the WT worms fed on the same bacteria or transgene worms in the absence of retinal (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by EPG recordings shown in Figure 8C and D.

claim: No photoinhibition of pharyngeal pumping was detected in wild-type worms or transgenic worms in the absence of retinal.
source: The onset of 470 nm illumination caused an immediate inhibition of pumping in such transgene worms but not in the WT worms fed on the same bacteria or transgene worms in the absence of retinal (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by EPG recordings shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The irradiance used in C. elegans experiments was insufficient to stimulate endogenous LITE-1 and GUR-3 UV/blue light receptors.
source: However, no photoinhibition was detected in the absence of retinal in either wild-type or transgenic worms. This indicates that the irradiance used in our experiments was insufficient to stimulate these endogenous photoreceptors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of photoinhibition in the absence of retinal.

claim: The magnitude of AnsACR-mediated photoinhibition of pharyngeal pumping depended on the irradiance.
source: The magnitude of the AnsACR-mediated photoinhibition depended on the irradiance (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response experiments shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The maximal irradiance (2.1 mW mm–2) completely abolished pharyngeal pumping for 15 s in all tested worms.
source: The maximal irradiance (2.1 mW mm–2) completely abolished the pumping for 15 s in all tested worms (n=13).
evidence: This is supported by EPG recordings at maximal irradiance.

claim: In five of 13 worms, individual action potentials were observed during the second half of 30 s illumination at maximal irradiance, indicating adaptation.
source: In five of 13 worms, individual action potentials were observed during the second half of the 30 s illumination period, an indication of adaptation.
evidence: This is supported by EPG recordings and represents an observation of adaptation.

claim: Two independently created transgenic C. elegans lines showed the same degree of photoinhibition.
source: Two independently created transgenic lines showed the same degree of photoinhibition (Figure 8E, filled and empty symbols).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of EPG recordings from two lines shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The photoinhibition of pharyngeal pumping was fully reversible: after switching off the maximal-irradiance light, the pumping frequency returned to the pre-illumination level with τ~9 s.
source: The photoinhibition was fully reversible: after switching off the maximal-irradiance light, the pumping frequency returned to the pre-illumination level with τ~9 s.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of EPG recordings after light offset.

claim: Eukaryotes acquired ChR genes at the early steps of their evolution.
source: Our identification and characterization of ChRs in ancyromonads, phylogenetically placed near the most commonly inferred root of the eukaryote tree (Brown et al., 2018), suggests that eukaryotes acquired ChR genes at the early steps of their evolution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic position of ancyromonads and the presence of ChRs in them.

claim: ChR genes or transcripts have been found only in protists that develop flagella at some stage of their life cycle.
source: Consistent with the role of the encoded proteins as phototaxis receptors as shown in C. reinhardtii, ChR genes or transcripts have been found only in protists that develop flagella at some stage of their life cycle.
evidence: This is stated as an observation consistent with the known function of ChRs.

claim: The diatom O. aurita loses flagella in the vegetative state but retains them in male gametes.
source: The diatom O. aurita, in which we identified ChRs, is no exception: the flagella are lost in the vegetative state of this protist but are still present in its male gametes (Nanjappa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on O. aurita biology.

claim: Prediction of biophysical properties such as ionic selectivity from protein sequences is a major unresolved problem in ChRs research.
source: Prediction of biophysical properties such as ionic selectivity from protein sequences is a major unresolved problem in ChRs research.
evidence: This is stated as a known challenge in the field.

claim: NlCCR shows ~29% identity and ~49% similarity in the 7TM domain to each of the two ancyromonad ACRs.
source: The NlCCR sequence shows ∼29% identity and ∼49% similarity in the 7TM domain to each of the two ancyromonad ACRs
evidence: This is a quantitative result from sequence comparison.

claim: In earlier known ChRs, the presence of conserved Glu residues in TM2 and the TM2-TM3 loop correlates with cation selectivity.
source: In the earlier known ChRs, the presence of conserved Glu residues in TM2 and the TM2-TM3 loop, corresponding to Glu82, Glu83, Glu90, and Glu101 of CrChR2, correlates with cation selectivity (Govorunova et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: TM2 of NlCCR contains no carboxylated residues, suggesting a unique mechanism of cation selection.
source: However, TM2 of NlCCR contains no carboxylated residues (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which suggests a unique mechanism of cation selection in this channel.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: NlCCR is a good candidate for optogenetic stimulation of neuronal activity with blue light.
source: NlCCR is the most blue-shifted among ancyromonad ChRs and generates larger photocurrents than the earlier known PsChR2 with a similar absorption maximum (Govorunova et al., 2013), which makes NlCCR a good candidate for optogenetic stimulation of neuronal activity with blue light.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spectral and functional properties of NlCCR.

claim: The retinal-binding pockets of all three ancyromonad ChRs contain residues corresponding to Met118 and Ala215 of bacteriorhodopsin, characteristic of red-shifted microbial rhodopsins.
source: Paradoxically, the retinal-binding pockets of all three ancyromonad ChRs contain the residues corresponding to Met118 and Ala215 of bacteriorhodopsin, the well-known 'color switches' characteristic of red-shifted microbial rhodopsins.
evidence: This is supported by sequence comparison shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The role of the near-ring Met118 homolog in red-shifting the spectrum has been experimentally verified in multiple rhodopsins.
source: The role of the near-ring Met118 homolog in red-shifting the spectrum has been experimentally verified in Haloquadratum walsbyi BR (Sudo et al., 2013), Gloeobacter violaceus rhodopsin (Engqvist et al., 2015), archaeorhodopsin-3 (Kato et al., 2015), and Chrimson (Oda et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The bulky Met side chain pushes away the C7 atom of retinal, increasing ring-chain coplanarity, expanding π-conjugation, and red-shifting absorbance.
source: It is thought that the bulky Met side chain pushes away the C7 atom of retinal, increasing the ring-chain coplanarity, expanding the π-conjugation, and red-shifting absorbance, as theoretically predicted in the GtACR1_C133M mutant (Tsujimura et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: The red-shifting effect of the Ala215 homolog has been demonstrated in multiple rhodopsins.
source: The red-shifting effect of the Ala215 homolog has been demonstrated in N. pharaonis sensory rhodopsin II (Shimono et al., 2000a), H. salinarum BR (Spudich et al., 2012), Chrimson (Oda et al., 2018), sodium-pumping rhodopsin KR2 (Inoue et al., 2019), and Mantoniella squamata ACR1 (Oppermann et al., 2024)
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The red-shifting effect of the Ala215 homolog is explained by electrostatic interactions between the polar residue in this position and the RSB.
source: and is explained by electrostatic interactions between the polar residue in this position and the RSB.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on established knowledge.

claim: Either the torsion around the C6-C7 bond is already enforced by a different geometry of the Met118 homolog in ancyromonad ChRs, or the blue-shifted absorbance arises by a different mechanism.
source: which suggests that either the torsion around the C6-C7 bond is already enforced by a different geometry of the Met118 homolog or that the blue-shifted absorbance of ancyromonad ChRs arises by a different mechanism.
evidence: This is speculation based on the unexpected mutational effects.

claim: Atomic structures of ancyromonad ChRs are needed to investigate the unexpected spectral shifts observed when mutating residues of the retinal binding pocket.
source: Atomic structures of ancyromonad ChRs are needed to investigate the unexpected spectral shifts we observed when mutating residues of the retinal binding pocket.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs based on the current findings.

claim: GtACRs can inhibit action potentials at the soma while triggering synaptic transmission due to high axonal Cl- reversal potential.
source: We previously showed that GtACRs could inhibit action potentials at the soma while triggering synaptic transmission due to high axonal Cl- reversal potential (Messier et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: AnsACR and FtACR showed similar phenomena to GtACRs in brain slice experiments, inhibiting action potentials while depolarizing axonal terminals.
source: AnsACR and FtACR showed similar phenomena in our brain slice experiments. These ACRs can inhibit action potentials in cortical neurons but depolarize axonal terminals and trigger synaptic transmission at the onset of light stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Fusing ancyromonad ACRs with somatodendritic trafficking motifs could lead to potent inhibition with reduced axonal excitation.
source: Fusing these new ACRs with somatodendritic trafficking motifs to reduce axonal expression (Mahn et al., 2018; Messier et al., 2018) could lead to potent inhibition with reduced axonal excitation.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future work based on previous strategies, supported by citations.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of C. elegans pharyngeal pumping has been demonstrated earlier using Mac or NpHR expressed in cholinergic neurons.
source: Optogenetic inhibition of C. elegans pharyngeal pumping has been demonstrated earlier upon expression of the Leptosphaeria maculans proton-pumping rhodopsin known as Mac (Trojanowski et al., 2014) or N. pharaonis halorhodopsin (NpHR) (Schüler et al., 2015) in the cholinergic neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Ion-pumping rhodopsins require almost 20 times higher irradiance for photoinhibition than the maximal irradiance used in this study.
source: However, ion-pumping rhodopsins such as these transport only one ion per absorbed photon and, therefore, require almost 20 times higher irradiance for photoinhibition than the maximal irradiance used in this study.
evidence: This is a comparison based on the known properties of ion pumps versus channels.

claim: All ACRs, including AnsACR, transport multiple anions during the open state and are more efficient optogenetic silencers than ion-pumping rhodopsins.
source: All ACRs, including AnsACR that we tested in the worms, transport multiple anions during the open state and, therefore, are more efficient optogenetic silencers than the ion-pumping rhodopsins.
evidence: This is stated as a general property of ACRs based on their mechanism of action.

claim: The C. elegans pharynx is innervated by 20 neurons, 10 of which are cholinergic.
source: The C. elegans pharynx is innervated by 20 neurons, 10 of which are cholinergic (Pereira et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on C. elegans anatomy.

claim: A pair of MC neurons is the most important for regulation of pharyngeal pumping in C. elegans.
source: A pair of MC neurons is the most important for regulation of pharyngeal pumping, but other pharyngeal cholinergic neurons, including I1, M2, and M4, also play a role (Trojanowski et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The pharyngeal muscles in C. elegans generate autonomous contractions in the presence of acetylcholine tonically released from the pharyngeal neurons.
source: Moreover, the pharyngeal muscles generate autonomous contractions in the presence of acetylcholine tonically released from the pharyngeal neurons (Trojanowski et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The blue-shifted absorption properties of ancyromonad ChRs hold promise for multiplexed applications alongside red-shifted indicators.
source: The blue-shifted absorption properties of ancyromonad ChRs hold promise for multiplexed applications alongside red-shifted indicators and warrant further evaluation across diverse experimental systems.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the potential applications of the characterized ChRs.
